title: Retrieval-augmented generation (preview)

sections.title: 18.4 BM25: keyword search that still works

html:
Purpose. An LLM does not know your documents. RAG lets it look them up before it answers, so its answers can be current, specific to your data, and backed by quotes. For the loan project it is how the copilot will answer questions about credit policy and the EBA guidelines.

This chapter is written ahead of the videos (Shaw Talebi's RAG video and IBM's overview are on the plan for Sunday 18 October), from Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval post and standard practice. It will be revised after you watch them.

Key ideas

  • RAG is an open-book exam: retrieve the relevant passages, put them in the prompt, and let the model answer from them with citations.
  • The pipeline: split documents into chunks, index them, retrieve the best few for a question, generate an answer that cites them.
  • Keyword search (BM25) and meaning search (embeddings) fail in different ways. Use both, and merge the rankings.
  • Measure retrieval separately from generation: hit@k asks "was the right passage among the top k?"

18.1 The idea

A model's knowledge is frozen at training time, and it has never seen your policy documents. You have three options. RAG hands it the right pages at question time: an open-book exam. Fine-tuning trains the knowledge into its weights: studying for a closed-book exam. That is worth it when knowledge must live in the model's head or the style has to change, and it is slower, costlier and harder to update. Long context puts the whole document in the prompt, which works for small corpora and gets slow and expensive for large ones. For a changing collection of documents where answers must cite their source, RAG is the default (Lewis et al., 2020, introduced the name).

18.2 The pipeline

  1. Load and clean the documents. Extract text from the PDF and check it. Tables and headers often come out broken.
  2. Chunk: split the text into passages. Too small and a passage loses its meaning; too large and the relevant sentence is diluted. A few hundred tokens with a little overlap is a typical start, cut at headings and paragraph breaks where possible. Keep metadata with each chunk (document, section, page), because that is what the citation will point to. (Anthropic's cost example assumes chunks of about 800 tokens.)
  3. Index each chunk twice: as an embedding and in a keyword index.
  4. Retrieve the top chunks for the question.
  5. Generate: put the question and the retrieved chunks in the prompt, and instruct the model to answer only from them, cite the chunk ids, and say "not found in the documents" when the answer is not there.
  6. Evaluate retrieval and answers separately.

18.3 Embeddings and cosine similarity

An embedding model turns a piece of text into a vector, so that texts with similar meaning get vectors pointing in similar directions (Chapter 15). Retrieval embeds the question, then ranks chunks by cosine similarity to it. Libraries such as sentence-transformers give you local embedding models. Embeddings are good at meaning ("how large a mortgage can I get" matches "maximum loan amount") and weak at exact strings such as codes, names and article numbers.

18.4 BM25: keyword search that still works

BM25 scores a chunk by the words it shares with the question. It rewards words that appear often in the chunk, rewards rare words more than common ones ("the" counts for nothing, "LTV" counts a lot), and corrects for chunk length. It is excellent at exact terms ("Article 7", a guideline number) and blind to synonyms. That is the mirror image of embeddings.

18.5 Hybrid search and rank fusion

Run both searches, then merge. Anthropic's post lists the steps: embed and BM25-index every chunk, search with both, combine and remove duplicates with a rank fusion method, and put the top K chunks in the prompt. A simple and popular fusion method is reciprocal rank fusion: each chunk earns 1 / (k + rank) from every list it appears in, with k = 60 by convention, and the sums decide the order.

import numpy as np

def cosine(a, b):
    return float(a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b)))

query = np.array([1.0, 0.0])
chunks = {"c1": np.array([1.0, 1.0]), "c2": np.array([0.9, 0.1]), "c3": np.array([0.0, 1.0])}
ranked = sorted(chunks, key=lambda c: cosine(query, chunks[c]), reverse=True)
print([(c, round(cosine(query, chunks[c]), 3)) for c in ranked])    # [('c2', 0.994), ('c1', 0.707), ('c3', 0.0)]

def rrf(rankings, k=60):
    scores = {}
    for ranking in rankings:                         # each ranking is a list of chunk ids, best first
        for rank, chunk_id in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
            scores[chunk_id] = scores.get(chunk_id, 0) + 1 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)

bm25 = ["c7", "c2", "c9"]
vectors = ["c2", "c5", "c7"]
print(rrf([bm25, vectors]))                          # ['c2', 'c7', 'c5', 'c9']

Chunk c2 is second in one list and first in the other, so it wins; c7 is first in one and third in the other, so it comes next. A chunk that appears in both lists beats one that appears in only one, even if that one ranked high.

18.6 Contextual retrieval and reranking

A chunk read alone can lose its meaning: "revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter" does not say which company or which quarter. Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval asks an LLM to write a short context (usually 50 to 100 tokens) for each chunk from the whole document, and prepends it to the chunk before embedding it and before building the BM25 index. On their test sets, the failure rate of retrieving the right chunk in the top 20 fell from 5.7% to 3.7% with contextual embeddings (35% fewer failures), to 2.9% when contextual BM25 was added too (49% fewer), and by 67% when a reranker was added on top. A reranker is a second model that re-scores the top candidates and keeps the best few (Anthropic took the top 150 from the first search and kept the top 20). Their one-time cost estimate was about $1.02 per million document tokens, using prompt caching, under their stated assumptions. These are their numbers on their data: measure on yours before you believe them.

18.7 Citations and refusing to guess

The prompt should say: use only the passages below; cite the chunk id after every claim; if the passages do not contain the answer, say so. Then check the citations in code: every cited id must be among the retrieved chunks, and, if you ask for quotes, each quote must appear in the chunk. An answer with a fake citation is worse than no answer. Also treat retrieved text as data, not as instructions: a document might contain the sentence "ignore your previous instructions" (prompt injection), and your system prompt must not obey it.

18.8 Measuring RAG

Evaluate retrieval first, because a perfect generator cannot answer from the wrong pages. Write about 20 questions, and for each one note the gold chunk or section that answers it. Then:

def hit_at_k(results, gold, k=5):
    return sum(g in r[:k] for r, g in zip(results, gold)) / len(gold)

results = [["c2", "c7", "c5"], ["c1", "c4", "c8"], ["c9", "c3", "c6"]]   # retrieved chunk ids for 3 questions
gold = ["c7", "c2", "c9"]                                              # the chunk that answers each question
print(round(hit_at_k(results, gold, k=3), 3), round(hit_at_k(results, gold, k=1), 3))   # 0.667 0.333

Hit@3 is 0.667 (two of three gold chunks were in the top three) and hit@1 is 0.333. Compare BM25 alone, embeddings alone and the hybrid on the same questions, and show the table. Then evaluate answers: is the answer correct against a gold answer, is every citation valid, and does the system refuse when the question has no answer in the documents? Include a few such unanswerable questions on purpose.

Loan example. The corpus is the EBA guidelines on loan origination plus a short synthetic credit policy with three rules you set yourself. A question like "What is our maximum loan-to-value for a first mortgage?" has one right passage in the synthetic policy, and an exact term to match. A question like "What do the EBA guidelines say about assessing creditworthiness?" needs meaning rather than exact words. A router decides whether a question goes to the database, to the policy search, or to both.

Common mistakes

  • Chunking blindly through the middle of sentences, tables or headings.
  • Using only embeddings and losing exact terms, or only BM25 and losing meaning.
  • Evaluating only the final answers: you cannot tell whether retrieval or generation failed.
  • Trusting citations without checking that they exist.
  • Never testing questions whose answer is not in the documents.

Check yourself

  • Why is hybrid search better than embeddings alone for a question about "Article 7"?
  • Compute the reciprocal rank fusion score of a chunk that is first in one list and third in another (k = 60).
  • What does contextual retrieval add to a chunk, and when?
  • Why measure hit@k before judging the generated answers?
Show answers

(1) Embeddings are weak on exact strings; BM25 matches the literal term. (2) 1/61 + 1/63 = 0.01639 + 0.01587 = 0.0323. (3) A short LLM-written description of where the chunk sits in its document, prepended before embedding and before BM25 indexing. (4) If the right passage is not retrieved, no generator can answer correctly, so retrieval is measured on its own first.
